footer.description: Real-time audio collaboration and secure demo sharing platform for music producers.

problem.title: Sending a demo shouldn't cost you the track.
problem.lead: Two things break every remote review: the file leaves your hands, and nobody hears the same second.

leak.label: Problem 01
leak.title: The file walks
leak.body: A WAV in an inbox is a WAV on somebody else's drive. Once it has been downloaded there is no version, no owner, and no way back.
leak.answer: Every master carries your voice, and every link expires.

drift.label: Problem 02
drift.title: The room drifts
drift.body: One person pauses, another seeks, a third hears the drop four seconds late. Notes stop being about the music and start being about timecode.
drift.answer: One playhead, one position, broadcast to the whole room.

pillars.title: Three modules, one workbench.
pillars.lead: A library that holds the work, a tag that signs it, and a room to play it in.

library.title: Library
library.description: Upload MP3, WAV or FLAC straight to storage and keep every take in one place.

voiceTag.title: Voice Tag
voiceTag.description: Write it or record it, then bake it into the master on a loop you control.
voiceTag.fact2: Or upload your own, up to 10s

liveRoom.title: Live Room
liveRoom.description: Share a six-character code and listen together, in step, with voice on top.
liveRoom.fact1: Play, pause and seek stay in sync

voiceTag.title: Your name, every thirty seconds.
voiceTag.lead: The tag is mixed into the master on the server, not layered on in the player — so what leaves the platform is already signed.
voiceTag.point1Body: Wavenet and Neural2 voices in Vietnamese, US English and UK English, male or female. Or upload a take of your own, up to ten seconds.
voiceTag.point2Title: Hear it before you keep it
voiceTag.point2Body: Preview any wording and voice together. Nothing is stored until you decide to save it.
voiceTag.point3Body: FFmpeg loops the tag, ducks the music underneath it and exports a new MP3 master. The settings are fixed at upload, so the result is reproducible.

liveRoom.title: Everyone on the same bar.
liveRoom.lead: The host holds the transport. Play, pause, seek and track changes go out over WebSocket, so the room hears one position — not five.
liveRoom.point1Body: Share a six-character code. Requests land in a waiting room, and nobody is inside until you let them in.
liveRoom.point2Body: Comments attach to a position on the timeline and surface as playback reaches them. No more “around 1:42, I think”.
liveRoom.point3Body: Peer-to-peer voice and video for up to seven people, negotiated through the server and carried directly between browsers.
liveRoom.commentSample: the low end fights the kick here

workflow.title: From upload to listening party in four moves.
workflow.step1Body: The file goes straight from your browser to storage over a signed, one-hour link. You watch a progress bar, not a spinner.
workflow.step2Body: Pick a voice tag, then set the interval, volume, ducking and start offset. Locked in at upload so the master stays reproducible.
workflow.step3Body: The job is queued and picked up by a worker that mixes the tag in with FFmpeg. Follow it from processing to ready — and retry if it fails.
workflow.step4Body: Open a room, send the code, approve who joins and press play. Everyone hears the same second.

trust.title: Boring where it matters.
trust.lead: The parts nobody puts in a demo, built anyway.
trust.item1Body: Every storage key is checked against the account that owns it before a file is read or written.
trust.item2Body: Playback runs on signed URLs valid from one minute to twenty-four hours, and they cannot be reused after that.
trust.item3Body: Refresh tokens rotate on every use, revoked ones are blacklisted, and you can end any active session yourself.
trust.item4Body: Closed accounts are anonymised by a scheduled job, and deleting a track clears its files from storage too.

hero.title: Three modules, one continuous workflow.
hero.lead: This page follows the order you will actually click: from the first demo file to a room listening together. How it works underneath gets a page of its own.

guide.title: From an empty library to a room listening together.
guide.lead: Pick a module to see the full flow. Every step is a real screen in the app.

library.title: Library
library.summary: Where every demo enters the system. Upload it, name it, and find it again even when you misremember the title.
library.step1Body: Once you are signed in, the whole library lives under Playlist in the nav. It starts empty.
library.step2Body: Drop or pick an MP3, WAV or FLAC up to 200 MB. The progress bar follows bytes actually sent, not an estimated animation.
library.step3Body: Title, artist, cover art. Skip the cover and a default one is used — it will not block you from saving.
library.step4Body: Search strips accents and tolerates typos, so a rough guess still lands on the right track.
library.tip1: Files over 200 MB are rejected in the browser — not a single byte of bandwidth is spent.
library.tip2: Closing the tab mid-upload loses the session; there is no resume yet.
library.tip3: The original file is always kept. A tagged version is saved as a separate copy.

voiceTag.title: Voice Tag
voiceTag.summary: Your audio signature, baked into the master on a loop interval you choose.
voiceTag.step1Body: Every tag you have made lives in one place, previewable straight from the list.
voiceTag.step2Body: Type text and have it spoken by a synthetic voice, or record and upload your own, up to 10 seconds.
voiceTag.step3Body: The preview runs the same processing pipeline as the final render, so what you hear is what you get.
voiceTag.step4Body: Pick a song, set the loop interval and the tag level, and a new version is rendered alongside the original.
voiceTag.tip1: The original is never overwritten — each bake produces a new file.
voiceTag.tip2: The tag level is matched to the song's, so it neither disappears nor cuts through.
voiceTag.tip3: A short 1–2 second tag on a sparse loop usually sits better than a long one.

liveRoom.title: Live Room
liveRoom.summary: A six-character code, up to seven people, one track at the same second — with voice on top.
liveRoom.step1Body: The owner sets a name and a headcount limit, and gets back a six-character code.
liveRoom.step2Body: Others enter the code and request to join. The owner sees the queue and approves or turns down each one.
liveRoom.step3Body: The owner picks a track from their library. Play, pause and seek stay in step for everyone.
liveRoom.step4Body: Unmute to speak, send chat, or pin a comment to the exact second of the track. The owner can mute remotely or remove someone.
liveRoom.tip1: Turned down three times by the owner and you can no longer request that room.
liveRoom.tip2: Reloading mid-track drops you back at the right playback position.
liveRoom.tip3: Ending a room can be undone: the music is paused, not lost.

bridge.lead: Every module above started from a specific constraint. The technical page walks through the problem, the approach taken, and what that approach cost.

technical.title: The three hardest problems, and how they were solved.
technical.lead: Not a stack list. Each case below is a real constraint hit while building, the approach taken, and what had to be given up to take it.

outro.title: Enough reading. Go listen.

library.title: Moving a 200 MB file without choking the API server
library.subtitle: Direct upload with presigned URLs, and search that survives a typo.
library.problem: Routing the file through the API server means every upload holds a thread and a buffer, and then the same bytes have to travel again to storage. All the user sees is a progress bar that does not move.
library.approach: The backend never touches a byte. It signs a short-lived URL, the browser uploads straight to object storage, and only once that succeeds does the backend write metadata.
library.detail1: Type and size are checked client-side before a URL is requested — a bad file is rejected before any bandwidth is spent.
library.detail2: Progress comes from the XHR progress event, so the percentage is bytes genuinely delivered.
library.detail3: Metadata is written in one transaction after the upload succeeds; a half-finished upload leaves no orphan row.
library.detail4: Search runs on Elasticsearch with an accent-folding analyzer and fuzzy matching, falling back to a PostgreSQL query when Elasticsearch is unreachable.
library.decision: No resumable uploads. Chunking, per-part state and orphan cleanup are three things to maintain forever, in exchange for very little at the scale of a single demo file.

voiceTag.title: Why a tag at 100% still sounded tiny
voiceTag.subtitle: Measure loudness to EBU R128, match the tag to the song, then mix.
voiceTag.problem: A mastered track sits around -9 to -12 LUFS. A voice tag — synthesized, or recorded on whatever the user had — sits around -20 to -27. That 10 to 15 dB gap meant the volume slider ran out of travel long before the tag was audible: 100% only ever meant "unchanged", never "as loud as the song".
voiceTag.approach: Measure the integrated loudness of both sources, work out the gain that puts the tag a fixed headroom above the song, and only then mix. After that the user's percentage finally does what its label promises.
voiceTag.detail1: FFmpeg pipeline: measure LUFS on both → apply gain to the tag → build the looped tag track → mix down to a new file.
voiceTag.detail2: The gain is clamped between −12 dB and +18 dB. Past that the correction does more harm than good: lifting a very quiet tag only surfaces its noise floor.
voiceTag.detail3: Anything below −60 LUFS is treated as unmeasurable rather than believed — near-silence reports a number that would ask for an absurd boost.
voiceTag.detail4: Synthesized and user-recorded voices share one path once they are WAV files; only the source step differs.
voiceTag.decision: Rendered server-side rather than assembled with the Web Audio API in the browser. The result has to be identical on every machine, and the final mix needs to exist as a file to be shareable.

liveRoom.title: Seven people, one track, the same second
liveRoom.subtitle: The server holds an anchor, not a stream. And nobody can listen in on anyone's signalling.
liveRoom.problem: Everyone is on a different connection with different latency, and anyone can reload mid-track. Pushing the playback position every second would be both expensive and still wrong.
liveRoom.approach: The server neither streams audio nor counts seconds. It holds an anchor: which track, at what position, as of when, playing or paused. Each client derives the live position from that anchor plus elapsed time.
liveRoom.detail1: No process ticks every second to write the position — state changes only when somebody presses a button.
liveRoom.detail2: One event carries the whole state; its type only tells a client whether the audio source needs reloading.
liveRoom.detail3: A sequence number on every event makes a late-arriving frame a harmless no-op instead of a jump backwards.
liveRoom.detail4: WebRTC signalling goes through a per-principal user queue rather than a shared topic — one member's SDP and ICE cannot be subscribed to by another.
liveRoom.decision: Ending a room pauses the music instead of clearing it, against the literal requirement. Undo has to restore the session whole — deleting the row would make music the one thing that did not come back.
